summary: Nonprofit fundraising SaaS, Software Engineer role, intuitive full-stack web applications with end-to-end ownership

motivation_letter.name: Goonja Gandhi
paragraphs: Face-to-face fundraising is one of the most labor-intensive channels in the nonprofit world, and its ROI is only visible when operational data comes back clean and consistent. What stands out to me about Tapraise is that it treats efficiency, transparency, and data quality as one integrated problem — not as separate dashboard features. That is also why the platform can serve both NGOs and agencies: the underlying need is the same, even though the operating models differ.

This resonates with how I think about software. I studied linguistic philosophy before becoming an engineer, and the habit I kept is to ask: what problem is this concept actually solving? A real-time dashboard is only useful if it changes a decision; a CRM export is only useful if the data in it can be trusted. So I tend to look at the seams between field input, live reporting, and backend integrations — because that is where meaning is lost or preserved.

In practice, I have spent five years working at that seam. At TCS, I led a team of five and reduced API calls by 40% by rethinking state management with RxJS — the goal was not optimization for its own sake, but keeping the interface responsive while data stayed consistent underneath. At Datapret, I worked on an accessibility-focused platform and raised WCAG compliance by 30%, which also taught me about data quality in a broader sense: if someone cannot complete a workflow, that is a broken data point too. More recently, I built NewsAlign, an AI fact-verification system using RAG pipelines, FAISS, and LLM reasoning. The central insight was that retrieval is not reasoning — a system needs the right data before it can produce a good answer, and that is a lesson I would bring directly to fundraising data.

I also notice Tapraise expanding beyond its NGO base into agencies and sales teams, with products like QR payments pulling field fundraising closer to real-time transactions. That direction makes the operational puzzle harder, which is exactly the kind of complexity I find worth working on. As a Software Engineer, I would bring frontend architecture, real-time data handling, and practical AI integration, but more importantly a habit of questioning what each feature is for. Software like this only works if the people in the field trust it; I want to help build that trust.
motivation_letter.closing: Thank you for considering my application. I look forward to the opportunity to discuss how I can contribute.

motivation_letter.name: Goonja Gandhi
paragraphs: Yuno's opening premise — that global payment infrastructure is broken because it is fragmented, not because it is complicated — is the kind of problem statement that drew me into engineering. Before I wrote a line of production code, I studied linguistic philosophy, and the question I carried out of that time is the one I still ask of every system: what problem is this concept actually solving? Yuno's answer — that orchestration, optimization, and protection belong in one unified layer rather than dozens of stitched-together providers — has a clarity most platforms never reach.

I built NewsAlign, an AI-powered fact verification system, where the central design lesson was that retrieval is not reasoning. Finding the right documents through semantic search and FAISS solved only half the problem; the harder half was making an LLM reason correctly over what was retrieved. Yuno's separation of orchestration from optimization reflects the same boundary — connecting a payment provider is different from routing transactions intelligently, and both are different from protecting against fraud. That is an architecture I have learned to respect in my own systems.

On the engineering side, I have spent five years building high-performance web applications where complexity has to stay invisible to the user. At TCS, leading a team of five developers, I reduced API calls by 40% through RxJS-based state management, achieved zero accessibility violations in QA, and delivered enterprise interfaces built for maintainability, scalability, and performance. A payments frontend carries a particular burden: merchants should feel the power of the infrastructure beneath without ever having to see its mechanics. That is the kind of surface I know how to build.

The Senior Web Developer role at Yuno sits at exactly this intersection — a platform redefining how payments work, an AI layer that needs thoughtful integration, and an interface that must feel effortless to the businesses building on it. I would bring frontend depth, a working understanding of AI system design, performance discipline, and the habit of asking what problem we are solving before choosing how to solve it. That habit, more than any single technology, is what I would want to contribute to Yuno.
